title: Food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a food-crop system that reliably increases persistent soil-carbon stocks while maintaining useful harvests. Crops would transfer carbon captured during growth belowground, and enough of that carbon would remain in soil to produce a measurable gain beyond what would have happened under a credible local baseline. The advance would combine crop traits and agricultural management with verification of the resulting storage.

The defining outcome is additional, durable storage, rather than simply larger roots or greater carbon inputs. More crop-derived carbon entering the soil does not by itself establish that total soil-carbon stocks have increased: the system must also account for losses of existing carbon. A claim of net climate benefit additionally requires accounting for greenhouse-gas emissions associated with producing and managing the crop. These distinctions define the proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability could make food production and verified carbon removal repeatable outputs of the same agricultural system. Its revolutionary significance would lie in maintaining useful harvests while adding persistent belowground carbon, potentially allowing existing agricultural land to contribute to carbon removal. This is a conditional impact argument: the supplied material does not quantify the suitable land area, achievable storage rate, or aggregate removal potential.

The direct consequence would be additional soil-carbon storage within the demonstrated operating conditions. A substantial climate contribution would depend on the magnitude and persistence of that storage, favorable full-system greenhouse-gas accounting, practical deployment, and reliable verification. Adoption across a large area could amplify the benefit, but neither broad deployment nor a particular global climate effect follows automatically from a successful field trial.

The carbon-removal analogy has limits. Increased root biomass is not equivalent to persistent soil-carbon accumulation, and soil storage should not be treated as an indefinitely expanding reservoir. Soil dependence, possible reversal, and an eventual approach to a new equilibrium are concerns identified in the supplied research that a demonstration program would need to evaluate; they were not independently substantiated by an inspected source in the supplied review.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable control over the path from crop-derived carbon inputs to additional soil-carbon stocks that persist under actual farming and climate conditions. A successful system would need to direct enough carbon into persistent soil pools without offsetting losses of pre-existing carbon, unacceptable harvest penalties, or greater emissions elsewhere. The supplied material identifies this as the target capability but does not establish its present absence through a comprehensive review of the field.

The central scientific barrier is connecting crop traits to the eventual fate of carbon in soil. Greater belowground allocation is an intermediate change; the required outcome is a lasting increase in soil-carbon stocks. The engineering challenge is to make that outcome repeatable across specified soils, climates, and management practices while preserving useful food production. These are design requirements inferred from the proposed concept, rather than experimentally resolved mechanisms documented in the supplied evidence.

Measurement and attribution are also essential barriers. A convincing system must distinguish crop-associated gains from background changes and sampling uncertainty, assess carbon through the relevant soil profile, and establish additionality against a credible baseline. Persistence and susceptibility to reversal must be assessed alongside yield, costs, and full-system emissions. A program would need explicit definitions of acceptable durability and performance before these requirements could become operational tests.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes an April 2026 Earth’s Future paper by Eric W. Slessarev, Jennifer Pett-Ridge, and colleagues, titled “Assessing the Effect of a Deep-Rooted Grass on Belowground Carbon Storage in Cultivated Land: Insights From a Multi-Site US Study.” According to that research summary, comparisons at 12 U.S. sites found more root carbon under deep-rooted perennial switchgrass than under neighboring annual crops, while the average effect on soil organic carbon was not statistically detectable. These are reported findings from the supplied research, not findings independently verified in the supplied review.

The source index contains the paper’s title and URL but no captured document artifacts. Consequently, the review could not inspect the abstract, plain-language summary, methods, results, or figures; verify the document’s identity and retained-copy completeness; or check the reported comparisons and statistical finding. The supplied summary provides no numerical effect sizes or uncertainty intervals. This access limitation leaves the report unverified here; it is not evidence that the reported result is false.

Taken as described, the study illustrates why root carbon and soil organic carbon must be evaluated separately. A statistically undetectable average soil-carbon response would not establish that the true response is exactly zero, but it also would not demonstrate a reliable positive gain. Moreover, the switchgrass comparison described in the research is not a demonstration of a food crop maintaining harvests while delivering durable, additional soil carbon and a verified net climate benefit.

The supplied evidence therefore does not establish completion of AGR-09. It also cannot support an exhaustive claim about the state of the field: the review records no evidence of research coverage through November 1, 2026. The April 2026 study report should be interpreted at its stated date, without assuming that it captures all subsequent developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: conduct independently replicated, long-running field comparisons of candidate food crops and their management against credible local baselines. Include multiple major food-crop systems and contrasting soil types, with climate and management conditions documented. Define trial duration, intended persistence, acceptable harvest performance, and the claimed deployment domain in advance. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated long-running field comparisons span crops and soils

completion_criteria.text: Measure whole-profile soil-carbon stock changes and their uncertainty, alongside root carbon where useful for interpreting the mechanism. Establish that any stock gain exceeds the baseline outcome and is not canceled by losses of existing carbon. Track useful harvests, full-system greenhouse-gas emissions, and costs so that a positive soil-carbon result can be distinguished from a practical food-production system with a net climate benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Whole-profile soil-carbon gains exceed baselines with full-system accounting

completion_criteria.text: Assess vulnerability to reversal under the management changes and climatic stresses relevant to intended use, and state what continued practices are required to retain the gains. Independent replication should establish where the result is repeatable and where it fails or remains uncertain. Finite trials would demonstrate breadth within tested conditions; they could not establish literal universality or guarantee indefinite retention.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes soil-carbon retention limits under relevant stresses

completion_criteria.text: No numerical storage-rate threshold is adopted here. The supplied research rejects a historical figure of 10–20 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year as either a demonstrated performance level or a necessary completion threshold, and the underlying historical list was not supplied. A proposed program should instead justify a practically meaningful rate, duration, and uncertainty bound for its intended scale of use.
completion_criteria.label: Practically meaningful storage rate, duration, and uncertainty bounds are justified

related_concepts.text: AGR-04, “High-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio,” has the closest overlap. A perennial grain could contribute both food production and belowground carbon inputs, but perenniality does not itself establish additional, persistent soil-carbon storage. AGR-04 concerns perennial grain production; AGR-09 concerns the verified carbon outcome while producing food. Either capability could advance without completing the other.

Conceptual comparison with AGR-01, “Cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation,” and AGR-02, “A transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops”: these target nitrogen supply and photosynthetic carbon capture, respectively. Both could interact with the productivity or emissions accounting of an AGR-09 system, but neither establishes the subsequent persistence of carbon in soil. Capturing more carbon in a crop and storing additional carbon durably belowground are distinct outcomes.

Conceptual comparison with AGR-03, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops,” AGR-06, “Rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity,” and AGR-07, “A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants”: these concern reproducing crop traits, maintaining crop health, and developing new crops. They could provide complementary capabilities for developing or deploying suitable food crops, but none substitutes for measuring additional soil-carbon storage, persistence, harvest performance, and net emissions.

Conceptual comparison with AGR-05, “Productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance,” and AGR-08, “Economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming”: these address saline-water production systems and farm operations. They could intersect with the environments or management of an AGR-09 deployment, but their defining achievements do not demonstrate durable soil-carbon gains. These relationships are synthesis from the supplied roster titles, not evidence that combined systems have been demonstrated.

unresolved_issues: The cited paper has no captured artifacts in the supplied source index. Its identity, reported findings, methods, effect sizes, uncertainty, and publication details remain unverified by the supplied review.
The evidence does not establish comprehensive research coverage through November 1, 2026, or support an exhaustive claim about whether the capability has been demonstrated elsewhere.
The supplied material does not quantify suitable agricultural area, achievable durable storage rates, deployment costs, or aggregate climate impact.
An actual demonstration program still needs operational definitions for trial duration, durability, acceptable harvest penalties, meaningful net removal, and reversal assessment.
Scientific assertions about soil dependence, reversal, and eventual equilibrium lack inspected supporting sources in this evidence package.
The historical source for the rejected 10–20 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year figure was not supplied.

brief.title: Food crops that leave lasting carbon in the soil
possible: Farmers could grow food while building a lasting store of carbon underground. Crop traits and farming practices would work together to keep more carbon in the soil than would have remained under usual local farming, while maintaining useful harvests.
why: Food production and measurable carbon removal could become repeatable outputs of the same farmland. Farmers could contribute to carbon removal through the crops they grow and the way they manage their fields.

sources.who: Eric W. Slessarev, Jennifer Pett-Ridge and colleagues
sources.showed: This study compared carbon belowground under deep-rooted switchgrass and neighboring annual crops.
sources.cited_for: The comparison supports the distinction between more carbon in roots and more carbon stored in soil.
sources.not_established: The comparison does not demonstrate a food crop that maintains harvests while delivering lasting extra soil carbon and a net climate benefit.

sources.showed: Crops supplied most of the carbon (C) entering the soil. Reduced soil turning and compost increased stored carbon near the surface, but deeper soil showed no gain.
sources.quote: C derived from crops was the main carbon input source over ten years.
sources.cited_for: Long-running farming trials can measure soil-carbon gains alongside crop contributions.
sources.not_established: Surface gains do not establish lasting storage deeper down or a net climate benefit after accounting for compost and other inputs.

sources.showed: The team traced carbon from rye grown between main crops. Carbon entering belowground initially remained more readily than carbon from shoots, but most was eventually lost from the soil.
sources.quote:
After 2 years, both above- and belowground inputs had declined substantially, indicating that the majority of
both root and shoot inputs are eventually mineralized.
sources.cited_for: Carbon entering soil through roots can persist initially yet still be lost later.
sources.not_established: Tracking rye carbon does not establish a lasting increase in total soil carbon or maintained food harvests.

shown: Wiebke Niether and colleagues measured higher soil-carbon stocks after ten years of reduced soil turning and compost use in German organic farming trials. The gains were concentrated near the surface; deeper soil showed no increase.

Eric W. Slessarev and colleagues reported more root carbon under switchgrass than neighboring annual crops, but no statistically detectable average gain in soil carbon. That leaves the size of any soil-carbon gain unresolved.
missing: A food-crop system must repeatedly add lasting soil carbon beyond a credible local comparison while maintaining useful harvests.
Measurements through the full soil depth must distinguish new storage from losses of carbon already present.
Independent trials must establish how long gains last and how farming changes or climate stresses can reverse them.
Storage gains must remain worthwhile after accounting for farming emissions, costs and continued management.

milestones.label: Independent long-running trials span food crops and soils
milestones.explanation: Independent, long-running trials would have to compare food crops and management across contrasting soils against usual local farming. This would test whether gains repeat while meeting defined harvest and storage goals.

milestones.label: Extra soil carbon survives full farm accounting
milestones.explanation: Measurements through the full soil depth would have to show extra carbon after existing-carbon losses, alongside harvests, farming emissions and costs. This would establish whether storage delivers a practical net climate benefit.

milestones.label: Independent trials establish when stored carbon stays or escapes
milestones.explanation: Independent trials would have to establish retention under relevant farming changes and climate stresses, including practices needed to keep gains. This would define where storage holds and where it can fail.

milestones.label: Useful storage rates and duration have justified uncertainty bounds
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would have to justify a useful storage rate and duration, with clear uncertainty bounds for its intended scale. This would establish practical value without assuming a universal target.

uncertain: How long must carbon remain stored, and what harvest reduction would still count as acceptable?
What storage rate would be useful at the intended scale, and how much farmland could achieve it?
How strongly would soil conditions limit gains, and when would further carbon accumulation level off?

page.title: Soil carbon sequestration by food crops
page.definition: A food-crop system maintains an additional soil organic carbon stock—carbon in soil organic matter—for at least 20 years, without reducing harvested food yield. Its greenhouse-gas balance remains net negative after accounting for farming inputs, emissions and displaced production; the 20-year duration is an Atlas fallback criterion.

goal.need: The National Academies reviewed cropland and grassland experiments showing carbon accumulation of 0.2–0.5 tonnes C per hectare per year over 20–40 years. Increasing root inputs does not guarantee such accumulation: across 12 US sites, switchgrass exceeded annual crops in root carbon, but its texture-corrected soil-carbon difference to approximately 1 m was 0.9 kg C per square metre, with a 95% confidence interval of −0.5 to +2.8.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
statements.quote: Increasing carbon allocation to roots without reducing above-ground yields will be a key issue for crop breeders, but is possible for several reasons.

statements.body: US Department of Energy, Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy
statements.quote: a 50 percent increase in soil carbon accumulation
statements.context: The ROOTS programme states this target for technologies and crop cultivars, alongside reduced nitrous oxide emissions and increased water productivity.

statements.quote: ROOTS will also measure whether deeper and stronger roots can increase durable soil carbon.
statements.context: Salk's soybean research project, announced on 22 September 2026, includes laboratory, greenhouse and field experiments.

completion.title: A food-crop system retains additional soil carbon for 20 years without reducing food yield.
completion.criterion: Independent field experiments demonstrate an additional soil organic carbon stock maintained for at least 20 years under specified continuing management. Stocks must increase absolutely and exceed the baseline change, with uncertainty excluding zero gain. Sampling must cover the soil profile affected by the intervention. Harvested food yield must equal or exceed the conventional comparator, and the greenhouse-gas balance must remain net negative after accounting for changed inputs, other emissions and displaced production. Root biomass or carbon entering soil alone does not satisfy the test.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback synthesis; no external document found defines this combined acceptance test.
completion.basis: Searched Salk HPI, ARPA-E ROOTS, NASEM, Verra VM0042 and XPRIZE for a combined food-yield, additionality and retention acceptance test; none was found. Salk specifies storage for decades and yields at least equal to current crops. XPRIZE instead specifies 100-year durability for general carbon removal. Twenty years is the Atlas's minimum literal interpretation of decades, not a published crop-certification threshold.

milestones.title: Crop belowground carbon has a soil-retention ratio greater than 1 relative to shoot carbon.
milestones.criterion: At a stated time after crop termination, divide the fraction of belowground carbon inputs remaining in soil by the fraction of shoot inputs remaining; a ratio greater than 1 establishes preferential belowground retention. Austin and colleagues used carbon-13 tracing in Michigan corn-system microplots, with five replicate blocks. Belowground rye inputs were about three times more likely to remain after five months. Most carbon from both sources was subsequently mineralized within two years; this result does not establish decadal storage.
milestones.set_by: Published root-versus-shoot retention diagnostic used by Austin and colleagues, following the field's relative-contribution-factor convention.
milestones.threshold_quote: a relative contribution factor greater than one indicates preferential storage

milestones.title: Food-crop soils exceed control carbon stocks with a 95% confidence interval wholly above zero.
milestones.criterion: The treatment-minus-control soil organic carbon stock difference over the sampled profile has a 95% confidence interval wholly above zero. Niether and colleagues reported approximately 16% higher stocks to 1 m under combined practices in two German trials, each with four blocks, after ten years; effects were confined to the upper 30 cm. Missing initial measurements to 1 m prevented calculation of sequestration since trial establishment. In the 12-site switchgrass comparison, the whole-profile difference did not exclude zero.
milestones.set_by: Statistical stock-comparison convention applied in Niether and colleagues' Figure 3 and Slessarev and colleagues' Figure 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: The difference from the control is significant when the confidence intervals do not cross the dashed line.

milestones.title: A food crop's root-trait improvements maintain or increase harvested yield.
milestones.criterion: After breeding material has been re-optimized, genetic improvements to root function are yield neutral or yield positive under comparable environmental conditions and best land management practices. ARPA-E publishes no numerical non-inferiority margin in this requirement. The German management experiments found no statistically significant difference in carbon exported through harvest over ten years; failure to detect a difference does not establish yield equivalence.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E ROOTS funding opportunity DE-FOA-0001565, Section I.E; the requirement concerns genetic improvements.
milestones.threshold_quote: All genetic improvements must be yield neutral or yield positive, once germplasm is re-optimized.

milestones.title: A food-crop system delivers positive net soil-carbon removals under Verra VM0042.
milestones.criterion: Implemented agricultural practices produce positive cumulative project carbon-stock change and positive additional net carbon dioxide removals under VM0042 v2.2, Sections 8.5–8.6, after the prescribed uncertainty and leakage deductions. Associated emissions enter the methodology's greenhouse-gas accounting. Direct soil-stock measurements use equivalent soil mass and cover at least 30 cm, or the impeding layer in shallower soils. Activities expected to cause sustained productivity reductions greater than 5% are excluded. This establishes removals for the assessed period, before the completion test's retention period.
milestones.set_by: Verra, VM0042 Improved Agricultural Land Management v2.2, incorporating corrections and clarifications issued on 11 June 2026.
milestones.threshold_quote: Carbon dioxide removals occur when the cumulative carbon stock change in the project scenario is positive

not_found: No external acceptance test was found that jointly specifies food-crop yield, additional soil-carbon storage and a measured decadal retention period.
No numerical yield-equivalence margin was found in the cited ARPA-E or Salk goals.
No inspected result established the combined completion criterion or independently verified removals attributable to Salk's enhanced-root food crops.
The EUR-Lex links for Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 redirected to the site's homepage, preventing inspection of the regulation.

results.finding: Two German field trials with four blocks each: combined practices yielded SOC stocks 16% higher than control to 1 m.
results.detail: The reported whole-profile difference has a 95% confidence interval above zero. Effects were concentrated above 30 cm; missing initial measurements to 1 m prevented calculation of sequestration since trial establishment.
results.quote: The highest SOC stocks (+ 16% compared with those of the control) were obtained when compost and mulch application were combined with reduced tillage (RT.M1C and RT.M3C).

results.finding: In five replicate blocks, rye belowground carbon was about 3 times as likely as shoot carbon to remain in soil after five months.
results.detail: The rye cover crop grew in a no-till continuous corn system. Most carbon from both sources was subsequently mineralized, so the result does not establish long-term storage.
results.quote:
Five months
following cover crop termination, belowground cover crop inputs were three times more likely to remain in soil
C pools than were aboveground inputs, and much of the root-derived C was in mineral-associated soil fractions.

results.finding: Dimorphic-root rice, four replicates across five environments, yielded 22% more grain than IR64 in 2024.
results.detail: The root-trait line was compared with IR64 under the same field conditions, but the text does not establish that breeding material was re-optimized or that best land management practices were used. At the severely nutrient-limited site, yield differences were not significant.
results.quote:
The grain yield of
DRO1

results.finding: Deep-rooting rice, 3 replicates per treatment: grain yield was approximately 10% higher than IR64.
results.detail: The lines were compared in one irrigated paddy field over two years, with and without fertilizer. The text does not establish that breeding material was re-optimized or that best land management practices were used.
results.quote: At maturity, Dro1-NIL showed approximately 10% higher grain yield than IR64, irrespective of fertilizer treatment.

results.finding: Root-specific OsNAC10 rice, 20 and 30 plants per line in successive seasons: grain yield rose 25%–42% under field drought versus controls.
results.detail: Three transgenic lines were tested over two seasons. The study reports increased root diameter and yield, but does not establish that breeding material was re-optimized or that the comparison used best land management practices.

results.finding: Cover-cropped annual systems (Reduced input and Biologically based; n=6 each) had significant 25-year whole-profile SOC gains of 11.0–11.5 Mg C ha−1 vs Conventional (SE ≈2).
results.detail: Table 5 reports Reduced input 11.0 ± 2.0 and Biologically based 11.5 ± 2.1 Mg C ha−1 gains over 25 years (n=6 each); these 95% CIs exclude zero. No-till 4.5 ± 2.5 does not clearly exclude zero.
results.quote: Change occurred at a lower rate in the annual row crops, but incremental additions at lower depths led to significant whole-profile gains.

results.finding: 25-year field experiment (4 rotations, 3 replicates) found SOC gain of 787 kg CO2 eq ha−1 yr−1 (range 310–1,280).
results.detail: Positive SOC change over time, but no untreated control or treatment-minus-control difference; no 95% CI wholly above zero; SOC discussion focused on 0–15 cm with 1979 baseline.
results.quote: During the 25-year period, the soils under these four rotation systems gained SOC equivalent to an amount of 787 CO2 eq ha−1 per year (ranging from 310 to 1,280 CO2 eq ha−1 per year).

results.finding: 25-year field experiment (4 rotations, 3 replicates) reported net sequestration of 0.027–0.377 kg CO2 eq per kg wheat grain.
results.detail: Shows net negative carbon footprint after crop-input emissions, but not calculated under Verra VM0042; no prescribed uncertainty/leakage deductions or equivalent-soil-mass 30 cm accounting.
results.quote: For each kg of wheat grain produced, a net 0.027–0.377 kg CO2 eq is sequestered into the soil.
